source.title: Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision
source.authors: A. Radford; Jong Wook Kim; Chris Hallacy; A. Ramesh; Gabriel Goh; S. Agarwal; G. Sastry; Amanda Askell; Pamela Mishkin; Jack Clark; G. Krueger; I. Sutskever

record.file_problem: The full paper is present; it is not visibly garbled or cut off.
record.tranche_reason: Tests downstream performance scaling in a new setting: vision-language image models, measuring zero-shot transfer error rather than language-model held-out loss.
record.gate_note: The paper cites language-model scaling work and reports a compute sweep for CLIP, but it does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy, token scaling, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Only the zero-shot transfer scaling results relevant to V6 are rows.
record.test_reason: Section 3.1.5 and Figure 9 check whether CLIP's downstream zero-shot error follows a log-log linear trend in model compute, as GPT-style scaling does. This is a downstream-predictability result (V6) for a new kind of system, a contrastive image-text model. It reports no pretraining loss, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors find that average zero-shot CLIP error scales smoothly (log-log linear) with model compute over 44x, like the GPT family. Individual evaluations are much noisier, and the authors cannot tell whether this reflects run-to-run variance or real non-monotonicity. The paper's overall conclusion is that the task-agnostic web-scale pretraining recipe from NLP transfers to vision.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses contrastive image-text pretraining and measures downstream zero-shot image-classification error; the original scaling-law studies concern language-model pretraining loss and compute allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The aggregate scaling trend is smooth, but performance on individual evaluations is much noisier and may be non-monotonic.
record.problems: The relevant scaling result is an aggregate over evaluations and covers a 44x compute range; individual task curves are noisier. The paper does not report held-out pretraining loss or numerical uncertainty for the aggregate trend.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported results left out.

untested.parts: Language models; downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss; any fitted exponent or extrapolation test. The paper's estimate that ~1000x more compute is needed to reach SOTA (Sec. 6) is a forecast, not a test.
Whether CLIP's pretraining (contrastive) loss follows a power law in parameters, data or compute. Only downstream error versus inference compute is reported.
Extrapolation of loss fits from small runs to large runs.
Architecture shape at fixed parameter count. ResNets scale width, depth and resolution jointly, and the ViT-versus-ResNet efficiency gap is not a fixed-parameter shape comparison.
Sensitivity of exponents or allocation to fitting choices.

missing.what: Per-dataset zero-shot accuracies for the 5 CLIP ResNets, which show non-monotonic or declining tasks (MNIST, KITTI, CLEVR) alongside steadily improving ones (ImageNet)

Average zero-shot score versus model GFLOPs, with and without prompt engineering. The ~5-point prompt gain is said to equal ~4x compute, a downstream scaling curve that depends on the evaluation method
Linear-probe average score versus forward-pass GFLOPs for CLIP ResNets and ViTs, which the authors say 'scale very well'

record.verdict_notes: CLIP is an image-text model, and 'compute' here is inference GFLOPs per image with fixed epochs and data, not training FLOPs. The link to V6, which concerns the language-model scaling claims, is therefore loose: the result is downstream scaling in a new modality and setting. No exponents, fits or uncertainty are reported for the scaling trend. The 0.82 correlation and 1.28 slope with confidence intervals in Sec. 3.1.5 concern zero-shot versus linear-probe performance, not scaling.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
The loss-minimising parameter/token allocation at fixed compute and its trend with compute.
Loss comparisons across architectures at fixed parameter count.
Whether held-out pretraining-loss power laws carry over to other modalities or training regimes; CLIP's result is about downstream zero-shot error.
The paper tests predictability of downstream performance with model compute for CLIP vision models, not language models or performance as a function of pretraining loss.
Whether loss exponents or compute-optimal allocations vary with fitting choices or setup.

rows.subject: CLIP ResNet models (RN50, RN101, RN50x4, RN50x16, RN50x64; reported as an aggregate)
rows.stage_stated: Pre-trained CLIP models; all trained for 32 epochs
rows.operation_detail: Compared average zero-shot error across models with differing compute.
rows.measure: Average zero-shot error as a function of model compute
rows.value: A smooth log-log linear trend across a 44x range of compute
rows.note: One aggregate result over five ResNet CLIP models; the paper describes the trend in the text and plots it in Figure 9.
rows.check: Link and state are right, with caveats. The compute axis is forward-pass GFLOPs per image (6.1 to 265.9, about 44x), not training compute. All models were trained for 32 epochs on the same data, so model size, depth, width and input resolution vary together. No exponent or fit statistic is given. The system is a vision-language model, not a language model, so this only partly matches the kind of system V6 names.

rows.subject: CLIP ResNet models (RN50, RN101, RN50x4, RN50x16, RN50x64; individual evaluations summarized)
rows.stage_stated: Pre-trained CLIP models; all trained for 32 epochs
rows.operation_detail: Examined zero-shot error trends on individual evaluations across model compute.

conditions.value: Individual evaluations among 39 evaluations across 36 datasets

rows.measure: Variation in individual-evaluation zero-shot error with compute
rows.value: Individual evaluations are much noisier than the overall trend; the authors are unsure whether this reflects run variance or non-monotonic performance on some tasks.
rows.uncertainty: The authors state they are unsure whether the variation is caused by run variance or genuine non-monotonicity.
rows.note: The paper reports this as a qualitative summary of individual evaluation curves, not separate numerical results for each task.
rows.check: State is reasonable, but the value is only qualitative. Table 11 gives per-dataset numbers that make it concrete. Zero-shot MNIST goes 66.6 to 59.3 from RN50 to RN101. KITTI goes 42.2 → 33.3 → 26.0 → 33.9 → 33.2, falling overall. CLEVR is non-monotonic (20.3, 28.1, 17.0, 17.6, 27.5). ImageNet rises steadily (59.6 to 73.6). Some tasks are closer to reversed than to noisy.

relationships.condition: Average zero-shot error over 39 evals on 36 datasets, 5 CLIP ResNets spanning about 44x model GFLOPs
relationships.reason: Aggregate error is well modelled by a smooth log-log linear trend in compute (r1, Fig. 9).
relationships.display_finding: Aggregate zero-shot error was well described by a smooth linear relationship between log error and log compute.

relationships.reason: Per-task curves are much noisier, and some are non-monotonic or decline. Table 11 shows this for MNIST, KITTI and CLEVR, so predictability holds for the average but not reliably per task (r2).
relationships.display_finding: MNIST, KITTI, and CLEVR exhibit noisy, sometimes non-monotonic or declining trajectories, making individual-task predictions less reliable than the average trend.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
